Before we start

Terms used in this deck

TermMeaningTermMeaning
HAZIDhazard identification: area-by-area checklist studyHAZOPhazard and operability study on the P&ID
MAHmajor accident hazardPFDprocess flow diagram (DTB-V1-PFD-201)
S, L, Rseverity 1–5, likelihood 1–5, risk $R = S\times L$ALARPas low as reasonably practicable
Preventionstops the cause becoming the eventMitigationlimits the harm after the event
FEEDfront-end engineering designLOPA, SILlayer of protection analysis; safety integrity level
HOLD, TBCdesign item not yet fixed; to be confirmedASammonium sulphate, (NH₄)₂SO₄

Tags follow ISA letters (LSHH = level switch high-high, FIC = flow controller). Every hazard, area and rank comes from the HAZID tab, register AS-SA-HZD-001 Rev A.

1

Part 1

What is a HAZID, and why are this unit's hazards mechanical?

Part 1 · the plan

Where HAZID sits and what it looks for

  1. HAZID against HAZOPtiming, drawing, prompt, output
  2. What can hurt on CR-201not fire or toxicity: vacuum, heat, solids, people
  3. The method in six stepsscope to further studies
  4. Prevention and mitigationthe two sides of a bow-tie

Step 1 · interactive · pick an aspect

Wide and early, then deep and detailed

HAZID works on the PFD in seven areas; HAZOP on the P&ID in nine nodes: HAZID decides what HAZOP must study in depth.

Step 2 · the material and the plant

Ammonium sulphate does not burn and is not toxic

Feature of CR-201Design numberHazard it creates
Body under vacuum106 m³ at 13.5 kPa aImplosion if not rated for full vacuum
Steam into the loopLP steam 3.5 bar a, relief on HOLDOverpressure of a 1 bar g vessel
Hot inventoryfeed 120 °C; loop 900 t/h at 62 °CScalds from leaks and plug clearing
Suspended solids17.5 t of crystals held upSettling, plugging, hard restart
People insidemanual descalingConfined-space entry, engulfment

Step 3 · interactive · walk the six steps

Six steps from scope to further studies

Existing controls are split before ranking: prevention lowers $L$, mitigation lowers what the event does.

Step 4 · interactive · pick a hazard

Each hazard has controls on both sides

H02 overpressure has alarms only on the left and nothing fitted on the right: a missing relief device is the gap.

Part 1 · summary

What Part 1 settled

  • HAZID is early, wide and coarse; HAZOP is late, deep and detailed.
  • On CR-201 the hazards are vacuum, overpressure, heat, solids and people.
  • Six steps: scope, areas, checklist, controls, rank, actions.
  • Controls split into prevention (left) and mitigation (right).

The method is set. Next: areas and guidewords make the search complete.

2

Part 2

How do areas and guidewords make the search systematic?

Part 2 · the plan

Divide the plant, then ask the same questions everywhere

  1. Seven study areasmarked on the PFD
  2. Twelve guideword categoriesnatural to organisational
  3. Area × guideword coveragewhere the hazards came from

Step 1 · interactive · pick an area

Seven areas on the PFD

Area A3, the crystallizer body, carries three of the four MAH: the vessel is the centre of the study.

Step 2 · interactive · pick a guideword

Twelve prompts asked in every area

Combustion gives no process hazard here, only hot work and lubricants: a checklist proves a category was asked, even when it gives little.

Step 3 · interactive · click a cell

Area × guideword: where the thirty hazards came from

Pressure and temperature (5), hot inventory, utilities and machines (4 each) give most hazards: every category produced at least one.

Part 2 · summary

What Part 2 settled

  • Seven areas follow the PFD: feed, loop, body, vacuum, product, steam, site.
  • Twelve guideword categories are asked in every area.
  • The coverage table shows every category was considered.

Thirty hazards are found. Next: rank them and pick the major ones.

3

Part 3

How are hazards ranked, and where does each one go next?

Part 3 · the plan

Rank, flag the major ones, pass them on

  1. The 5 × 5 risk matrix$R = S\times L$, four bands
  2. Re-ranking a hazardwhat a better control buys
  3. Major accident hazardsfour on CR-201
  4. From HAZID to other studiesHAZOP, LOPA, permits, layout

Step 1 · the ranking rule

Risk is severity times likelihood

$S$
severity of the worst credible outcome, 1 negligible … 5 catastrophic
–
$L$
likelihood with existing controls, 1 remote (< 10⁻⁴/yr) … 5 frequent (> 0.1/yr)
–
$$R = S \times L \qquad 1\text{–}4\ \text{Low},\ 5\text{–}9\ \text{Medium},\ 10\text{–}16\ \text{High},\ 20\text{–}25\ \text{Very high}$$

A teaching matrix, shared with the HAZOP tab.

Step 1 · interactive · click a cell

Where the thirty hazards fall

23 Medium, 6 Low, 1 High and none Very high: a plausible spread after the existing controls.

Step 2 · interactive · move S and L

What would a better control buy?

Prevention moves $L$, mitigation moves $S$: a High hazard needs a step on either axis to reach Medium.

Step 3 · interactive · pick a MAH

Four major accident hazards, none chemical

Two concern the vessel, two concern people at work on it: only H19, confined-space entry, ranks High.

Step 4 · interactive · pick a route

Each hazard leaves the HAZID with an owner

Process hazards become HAZOP nodes; H02 goes on to LOPA: HAZID opens studies, it does not close them.

Part 3 · summary

What Part 3 settled

  • $R = S\times L$ on a 5 × 5 matrix with four bands.
  • Prevention lowers $L$; mitigation lowers $S$.
  • Four MAH: implosion, overpressure, confined space, dropped object.
  • Every action goes to an owner: HAZOP, LOPA, permits or layout.

The register is the start: the HAZOP tab studies each process hazard node by node.

This deck

Key Takeaways

1

Do a HAZID early, on the PFD, area by area with a fixed checklist.

2

On CR-201 the major hazards are mechanical and human, not chemical.

3

Split controls into prevention and mitigation before ranking.

4

Fit the relief device of CR-201: overpressure has no mitigation today.
